rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Joseph is called truthful either because he interpreted the earlier dream truthfully or because the wine carrier never saw him lie in prison.
rows.anchor: the fact that he had never seen Joseph tell a lie during their time together in prison (R; see also 12:36c)

rows.speaker: My
rows.claim: The wine carrier may mean that the king and his notables will learn Joseph’s interpretation of the king’s dream.
rows.anchor: king and his notables might come to know of his interpretation of the king’s dream (My)

rows.speaker: My, Ṭs
rows.claim: Alternatively, the wine carrier may hope the king learns Joseph’s true rank and knowledge and releases him.
rows.anchor: or of Joseph’s true rank and knowledge and thus release him from prison (My,Ṭs)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph sees the request as a chance to impress the king with his interpretation and gain freedom.
rows.anchor: Joseph saw this as an opportunity to impress the king by interpreting the dream so that he could be set free

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph also wants to help the king because the dream signals an agricultural crisis for Egypt.
rows.anchor: a part of the dream signaled an agricultural crisis for the people of Egypt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The main reading makes Joseph the speaker, seeking to clear himself of blame before Potiphar.
rows.anchor: The speaker here is Joseph, who seeks to absolve himself of any blame before Potiphar

rows.speaker: Kl, R, Ṭs
rows.claim: An alternative interpretation makes Zulaykhā the speaker.
rows.anchor: speaker here could be Zulaykhā(Kl, R, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: IK, R
rows.claim: Some commentators identify Zulaykhā, rather than Joseph, as the speaker.
rows.anchor: some have argued that the speaker here is Zulaykhā (IK, R)

rows.speaker: Bḍ, Bg, Kl, Q, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Most commentators identify Joseph as speaker and treat this as a continuation of his words in 12:52.
rows.anchor: majority of commentators see these words as Joseph’s (Bḍ, Bg, Kl, Q, Ṭs, Z)

rows.speaker: Kl
rows.claim: Joseph says he does not absolve himself out of humility.
rows.anchor: I absolve not my own soul out of humility (Kl)

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: Joseph wants to emphasize that God protected him from falling into sin.
rows.anchor: God Who protected him from falling into sin (Bḍ; see 12:24c)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse grounds Muslim moral psychology in three Quranically described levels of the soul.
rows.anchor: plays a foundational role in the Muslim understanding of moral psychology and the structure of the human soul

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commanding soul calls people to base desires and actions that produce forgetfulness of God and violate His command.
rows.anchor: calls a person to submit to his or her base desires, and to those thoughts and actions that lead to forgetfulness of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blaming soul reproaches evil and forgetfulness while trying to change the person for the better.
rows.anchor: reproaches a person for his or her evil states and forgetfulness of God, while actively attempting to effect change

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The soul at peace has conquered the lower self and rests in remembrance of God, content and pleasing to Him.
rows.anchor: has conquered the lower self and resides in peace in the remembrance of God, returning to God content

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: After summoning and speaking with Joseph, the king recognizes his intelligence, wisdom, and virtue, reserves his abilities, and appoints him over the storehouses.
rows.anchor: the king realizes his intelligence, wisdom, and virtue (Q, Ṭ); he then expresses a desire to reserve Joseph’s abilities exclusively for himself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s establishment in Egypt follows a period of trial and hardship, as did the earlier establishment in 12:21.
rows.anchor: comes after Joseph undergoes a period of trial and hardship

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In 12:21 establishment lets God teach Joseph dream interpretation; here it lets him settle wherever he wishes, linking the two episodes.
rows.anchor: The purpose of establishing Joseph in Egypt in v. 21 is so that God might teach him the interpretation of events—that is, dreams

rows.speaker: Kā
rows.claim: Joseph’s freedom to settle anywhere can mean he could make his home in any Egyptian city because he controlled them all.
rows.anchor: “establish his home in any of Egypt’s cities because of his control over all of them” (Kā)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is also said that after Potiphar died, the king gave Joseph Potiphar’s former treasury position, conferring the title ʿAzīz.
rows.anchor: when Potiphar died, the king of Egypt gave Joseph Potiphar’s former position of being in charge of the treasury of Egypt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God does not neglect the reward of the virtuous; the reward of the Hereafter is greater than worldly reward and this world is only diversion and play.
rows.anchor: the life of this world is naught but diversion and play, whereas the Abode of the Hereafter is life indeed

rows.speaker: Bḍ, Kl
rows.claim: Famine had spread from Egypt to Canaan, so the brothers came to buy provisions stored during Egypt’s seven prosperous agricultural years.
rows.anchor: the famine that had afflicted Egypt had also affected Canaan

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: They failed to recognize Joseph because time had passed, his rich Egyptian clothing and status awed them, and they assumed he had died in the well.
rows.anchor: a long period of time had elapsed since they last saw him. Moreover, he now stood before them adorned in rich Egyptian garments

rows.speaker: Kl
rows.claim: The provisions are the food the brothers purchased from Joseph.
rows.anchor: Provisions here denotes the food that the brothers had purchased from Joseph (Kl)

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: The brother Joseph requests is Benjamin, though the Quran does not name him.
rows.anchor: considered by commentators to be Benjamin (JJ; see 12:8c), although his name is not mentioned in the Quran

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The ten brothers brought eleven camels and sought eleven food loads, ten for themselves and one for Benjamin, who remained home; Joseph wanted proof of the extra dependent during scarcity.
rows.anchor: The ten brothers who came to Egypt brought with them eleven camels and were requesting eleven camel-loads of food

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Joseph’s question subtly denies the extra load without directly accusing the brothers of wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: a subtle way of denying the brothers their request without accusing them of wrongdoing (R)

rows.speaker: Bg
rows.claim: Joseph says he will refuse future dealings and even bar them from the city unless they bring Benjamin, since their request otherwise implies a lie about an extra load.
rows.anchor: he would not do business with them; nor would they even be allowed to enter the city (Bg)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers promise to bring their eleventh brother next time because they expect to need more Egyptian food.
rows.anchor: they knew they would need to come to Egypt for more food in the future

rows.speaker: Bg, Z
rows.claim: Their merchandise may mean goods the brothers offered Joseph in exchange for food.
rows.anchor: goods that the brothers had presented to Joseph in exchange for food (Bg, Z)

rows.speaker: JJ, My, Ṭ
rows.claim: Alternatively, merchandise means the actual price the brothers paid for the food.
rows.anchor: the brothers paid for the food (JJ, My, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph returns everything to build their trust and draw them back with Benjamin.
rows.anchor: Joseph sought to gain their confidence and reliance upon him for future transactions

rows.speaker: My, Bg
rows.claim: The withheld measure is the remaining eleventh camel-load; obtaining the measure means obtaining the full amount of food they sought.
rows.anchor: the rest of the food that the brothers sought to acquire (My)

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: Jacob’s reference to the brother entrusted before means Joseph.
rows.anchor: His brother is a reference to Joseph (JJ; see 12:15c)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Calling God the best keeper expresses Jacob’s trust in God and resignation of the affair to Him.
rows.anchor: God is the best of keepers implies Jacob’s trust in God and his resignation of the whole affair to Him (Aj)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description of God as most Merciful of the merciful also appears in 12:92, 7:151, and 21:83.
rows.anchor: For God as the most Merciful of the merciful, see also v. 92; 7:151; 21:83

rows.speaker: Bg
rows.claim: The brothers use Joseph’s returned goods as goodwill to persuade Jacob to let Benjamin travel, since Benjamin’s presence is necessary to obtain more food.
rows.anchor: the brothers appeal to Joseph’s gesture of goodwill in order to convince Jacob to allow them to take Benjamin

rows.speaker: Kl
rows.claim: The meager rations are their existing ten camel-loads, insufficient to sustain the family for long.
rows.anchor: which was not enough to sustain them for long (Kl)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob requires a solemn pledge to return Benjamin, as he earlier did for Joseph.
rows.anchor: Jacob has his sons make a solemn pledge that they will return Benjamin to him, as he did earlier with Joseph

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: The exception unless surrounded is a general caveat for a situation in which they cannot fulfill the oath.
rows.anchor: “unless you come to a situation in which you cannot uphold the oath” (JJ)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: God as Guardian over their words means that God witnesses the oath.
rows.anchor: God is a witness to the oath (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same oath formula appears when Moses makes an oath with his future father-in-law.
rows.anchor: The same statement is uttered by Moses in 28:28 when he takes an oath with his future father-in-law

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Jacob’s advice to enter separately is interpreted as protection from the evil eye, associated with envy and bad omens.
rows.anchor: Jacob’s advice to his sons to enter by separate gates was given to help them avoid the evil eye (R)

rows.speaker: Bḍ, N, Aj
rows.claim: This reading says the handsome brothers had suffered the evil eye before and should avoid entering Egypt together conspicuously.
rows.anchor: since they were very handsome (Bḍ, N) and had fallen victim to the evil eye the last time they were there (Aj)

rows.speaker: other commentators
rows.claim: Other commentators read the advice as practical caution against attracting attention, hostility, or jealousy because the brothers were recognizable.
rows.anchor: Other commentators do not associate this verse with a fear of the evil eye, but simply with practical caution against attracting unwanted attention

rows.speaker: Bḍ, Z
rows.claim: Jacob admits his precautions cannot save his sons from what God has destined for them.
rows.anchor: despite Jacob’s advice to his sons, they cannot escape what God has destined for them (Bḍ, Z)

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: The separate entry could not prevent a major trial that the brothers soon faced.
rows.anchor: they would nonetheless soon undergo a major trial (Bḍ; see vv. 70–82)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Following Jacob’s advice fulfilled a need in his soul by assuaging his fear of losing his children.
rows.anchor: Jacob’s advice to his sons, along with their acceptance of it, was a means to assuage Jacob’s fear of losing his children (R)

rows.speaker: IK, Kl
rows.claim: Joseph honors his brothers, privately tells Benjamin that they are brothers, and explains what happened to him.
rows.anchor: He managed to inform Benjamin in private that he was his brother (IK, Kl) and explained all that had happened to him

rows.speaker: Bg
rows.claim: Joseph comforts Benjamin that the brothers’ past actions are over and occurred according to God’s Will.
rows.anchor: these events were in the past and according to God’s Will (Bg)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Joseph asked Benjamin not to tell the other brothers about their private meeting.
rows.anchor: He also asked Benjamin not to mention their private meeting to the other brothers (IK)

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathīr
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr says Joseph and Benjamin devised the plan that would keep Benjamin with Joseph.
rows.anchor: Ibn Kathīr states that Joseph and Benjamin then devised a plan that would ensure that Benjamin would remain with him

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī instead says Benjamin did not know the plan.
rows.anchor: al-Ṭabarī, however, says that the plan was not known to Benjamin

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The brother whose bag held the cup is Benjamin, and the cup was the king’s goblet.
rows.anchor: His brother’s saddlebag means Benjamin’s bag, filled with his belongings (Ṭ). As mentioned in v. 72, the drinking cup was the goblet of the king

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The king’s goblet served both for drinking and for measuring food; it was said to be gold set with jewels.
rows.anchor: used by him not only for drinking, but also for measuring food (Ṭ); it is said to have been made of gold and studded with jewels (JJ)

rows.speaker: Aj, Kl
rows.claim: Because Jacob distanced anyone caught stealing, Joseph placed the cup in Benjamin’s bag to make him appear culpable.
rows.anchor: Joseph placed the goblet in Benjamin’s bag, because that would make Benjamin appear to be culpable for the “crime” (Aj, Kl)

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Joseph’s companions said the goblet was missing; the herald offered a camel-load of food to whoever produced it, and guaranteed the reward.
rows.anchor: Joseph’s companions were the ones who said, We are missing the goblet of the king (Ṭs), but the declaration for a camel-load of food

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers’ proposed recompense means the person with the cup is surrendered to Joseph and his entourage for punishment.
rows.anchor: by being given over by the brothers to Joseph and his entourage

rows.speaker: Th
rows.claim: The brothers’ custom was to give a thief to the person robbed, just as the thief took that person’s property; the brothers then allowed a bag search.
rows.anchor: this was the brothers’ custom when dealing with thieves, namely, to give the thief over to the one from whom he had stolen

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: The divinely revealed plan to put the cup in Benjamin’s bag ultimately serves God’s solicitude for Joseph’s brothers.
rows.anchor: ultimate goal of the plot was for God to show His Solicitude to Joseph’s brothers (Aj)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Some say the king’s theft penalty was beating and charging double the item’s value, which would not let Joseph retain Benjamin after punishment.
rows.anchor: if someone was caught stealing, the person would be physically beaten for the crime and then charged double the worth of the item

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: God arranged for the brothers to invoke their own theft custom, allowing Joseph to retain Benjamin as planned.
rows.anchor: God willed that the brothers would themselves put forward the punishment for theft according to their own custom

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The degrees of knowledge relate to God’s raising of ranks and are linked to 6:83 and 40:15.
rows.anchor: For We raise in degrees whomsoever We will, see 6:83c; see also 40:15

rows.speaker: R, Aj
rows.claim: Joseph knew more than his brothers, yet all knowledge ultimately belongs to God the Knower.
rows.anchor: Joseph had more knowledge than they (R), and that all knowledge ends with God (Aj)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: More generally, human knowledge has a hierarchy, with a higher degree always possible and God’s knowledge highest.
rows.anchor: no matter how much knowledge a human being gains, there is always a higher degree of knowledge, the highest of which is God’s Knowledge

rows.speaker: IK, JJ, R
rows.claim: The accusation that Joseph had stolen refers to his reported theft and destruction of an idol from his maternal grandfather so it would not be worshipped.
rows.anchor: is said to have stolen an idol from his maternal grandfather and destroyed it, lest it be worshipped (IK, JJ, R)

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Joseph kept his retort that the brothers were worse to himself rather than saying it aloud.
rows.anchor: his response to his brothers, You are in a worse position, which he said to himself and did not voice aloud (Z)

rows.speaker: JJ, Z
rows.claim: Joseph meant that the brothers were worse because they had taken him from his father and treated him unjustly, while Benjamin had not joined in.
rows.anchor: the brothers were in a worse position than Benjamin, since they stole him (Joseph) from their father and treated him unjustly

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: The brothers invoke Jacob’s age, love for Benjamin, and reliance on him for solace after Joseph’s loss to explain his grief.
rows.anchor: Jacob loves Benjamin more than them, and that since Benjamin has been a means of solace for Jacob in place of Joseph

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The eldest brother is Reuben, though the Quran does not name him.
rows.anchor: The eldest of them refers to Reuben (not named in the Quran, but recorded as such in the commentaries

rows.speaker: Bg, Ṭs
rows.claim: Neglecting Joseph means failing to care for him and, by extension, breaking their pledge to return him safely.
rows.anchor: they failed to take care of him (Bg, Ṭs) and, by extension, when they broke the vow

rows.speaker: Bg
rows.claim: Reuben will remain in Egypt until Jacob calls him home or God decides whether Benjamin returns or Reuben goes home without him.
rows.anchor: God renders judgment upon him, referring to God’s Decision to return Benjamin to him or to send him back home without Benjamin (Bg)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The best-judge expression and related Quranic formulations are discussed at 7:87.
rows.anchor: For God as the best of judges and other cognate expressions in the Quran, see 7:87c

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Not being keepers of the unseen means they could not have anticipated Benjamin’s theft when they pledged, so they invoke Jacob’s exception to excuse the broken oath.
rows.anchor: there was no way the brothers could have foreseen that Benjamin would “steal” in Egypt when they made their pact with Jacob (Z)

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: The town means Egypt’s people, while the caravan means the people of Canaan.
rows.anchor: The town refers to the people of Egypt, and the caravan to the people of Canaan (JJ)

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: It is said that the people of Canaan testified to the brothers’ truthfulness when they returned to Jacob.
rows.anchor: they testified to the brothers’truthfulness (JJ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob’s words resemble his response to Joseph’s loss in 12:18.
rows.anchor: Jacob’s words here are similar to his response to the news of the loss of Joseph in v. 18

rows.speaker: Kl
rows.claim: The people Jacob hopes God will bring back together are Joseph, Benjamin, and Reuben, still in Egypt; the statement prophesies Joseph’s survival.
rows.anchor: The pronoun them refers to Joseph, Benjamin, and Reuben, who were still in Egypt

rows.speaker: My
rows.claim: One view says Jacob wept until he became blind from grief.
rows.anchor: in his sadness, Jacob wept so much that he went blind (My)

rows.speaker: Kl
rows.claim: Another view says his eyesight became very weak, as indicated by his eyes turning white.
rows.anchor: his eyesight became very weak (Kl), which is indicated by the words his eyes had turned white

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: The brothers ask from love and compassion for Jacob, figuratively expressing fear he will die if he continues grieving.
rows.anchor: motivated by love and compassion for their father (Ṭs), is a figurative way of telling him that they fear for his demise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob’s complaint only to God recalls his beautiful patience in 12:18 and 12:83, defined as complaining about suffering only to God.
rows.anchor: a form of patience in which one complains only to God about one’s suffering and not to other human beings

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Some interpret Jacob’s knowledge from God as intuitive knowledge that Joseph was still alive.
rows.anchor: interpreted by some to refer to Jacob’s intuitive knowledge that Joseph was still alive (R)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Jacob sends his sons to seek Benjamin, who is held, and Joseph, whom he believes survived because of a dream or a message from the Angel of Death.
rows.anchor: he believed Joseph was still alive, because he had either seen this in a dream or been informed by the Angel of Death

rows.speaker: JJ, N
rows.claim: Despairing of God’s comfort means losing hope in His mercy; forgiveness for the brothers appears in 12:92 and 12:97.
rows.anchor: not lose hope in God’s Mercy (JJ, N; for their forgiveness, see vv. 92, 97)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse resembles 39:53, which urges people not to despair of God’s mercy and promises forgiveness.
rows.anchor: This verse is similar in meaning to 39:53: Despair not of God’s Mercy. Truly God forgives all sins

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers return to seek Joseph and Benjamin as Jacob requested, without yet recognizing Joseph.
rows.anchor: The brothers went to Egypt in order to inquire about Joseph and Benjamin in accordance with Jacob’s wishes

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: Their affliction means intense hunger, and their meager merchandise means the few trade goods they brought for food.
rows.anchor: their intense hunger (Bḍ), as well as their meager merchandise, referring to what little goods they had with them to trade for food

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The appeal to charity is understood as a request that Joseph return Benjamin.
rows.anchor: And be charitable unto us is understood as a request for the return of Benjamin (Q)

rows.speaker: Kl
rows.claim: Joseph’s no-reproach statement is called a beautiful form of forgiveness; reproach may also mean physical punishment.
rows.anchor: There is no reproach against you this day is described in some sources as “a beautiful form of forgiveness”(Kl)

rows.speaker: Prophet Muhammad
rows.claim: At the conquest of Mecca, the Prophet cited Joseph’s forgiveness, then freed Quraysh after they acknowledged his noble status.
rows.anchor: “Verily I say to you as Joseph said to his brothers: there is no reproach against you

rows.speaker: Kl, My
rows.claim: Joseph’s instruction to place his shirt on Jacob’s face is said to rest on divine inspiration; the shirt is identified as paradise silk Gabriel brought to Joseph in the well.
rows.anchor: shirt cast over Jacob’s face was reportedly based on Divine inspiration (Kl, My). The shirt is said to be the same shirt made from the silk of Paradise

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: By calling Jacob astray, the brothers mean his excessive love for Joseph and hope to meet him, which they think unreasonable.
rows.anchor: the brothers mean Jacob’s overabundant love for Joseph and his hope to meet with him, which they thought unreasonable

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: The bearer of glad tidings carrying Joseph’s shirt was the brother who had earlier intervened against the plot to kill Joseph.
rows.anchor: the same brother (see 12:10c; JJ) who had earlier interceded with the brothers when they plotted to kill Joseph

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob’s question recalls what he announced in 12:85–86.
rows.anchor: For Jacob’s question, see his announcement in 12:85–86c

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: This exchange happened after the brothers returned home from Egypt.
rows.anchor: This conversation occurred after the brothers returned home from Egypt (Q)

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: Some say Jacob delayed seeking forgiveness, perhaps to see whether his sons were sincere and truthful.
rows.anchor: Jacob delayed his prayer for forgiveness a certain period of time (Q, R), perhaps to ascertain whether they were being sincere and truthful

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise to enter Egypt securely echoes the promise that Muhammad and his followers would enter the Sacred Mosque securely.
rows.anchor: with reference to the Prophet Muhammad and his followers, see 48:27, which states that the Muslims shall enter the Sacred Mosque in security

rows.speaker: JJ, Kl
rows.claim: Joseph raised his parents by seating them on the king’s throne.
rows.anchor: Joseph raised his parents up to the throne; that is, he seated them (JJ) upon the king’s throne (Kl)

rows.speaker: N
rows.claim: All who prostrated were Joseph’s parents and eleven brothers, corresponding to the sun, moon, and eleven stars in his vision.
rows.anchor: They [all] refers to Joseph’s parents and his eleven brothers, which correspond to the sun, the moon, and the eleven stars

rows.speaker: N
rows.claim: Prostration toward someone was a greeting and honor, like standing respectfully or kissing a hand.
rows.anchor: Prostrating toward someone was a way of greeting and honoring that person, much like standing up for someone out of respect or kissing the hand (N)

rows.speaker: N
rows.claim: Joseph omits the well and mentions prison because he had already forgiven his brothers.
rows.anchor: does not mention the well from which he was delivered, only the prison, since he had already told his brothers in v. 92

rows.speaker: Qu
rows.claim: Blaming Satan for discord between Joseph and his brothers amounts to excusing their wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: making an excuse for them for their wrong actions (Qu; see also 12:89–90c)

rows.speaker: N
rows.claim: Calling God Subtle means the manner in which He carries out His Will is subtle.
rows.anchor: the manner in which God carries out His Will is subtle (N)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph held the highest standing in Egypt below the king, which explains his having some sovereignty.
rows.anchor: Joseph was granted something of sovereignty since he had the highest standing in Egypt next to the king

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God as Originator of the heavens and earth is linked to 2:117, 6:14, 6:101, 35:1, 39:46, and 42:11.
rows.anchor: For God as the Originator of the heavens and the earth, see 2:117; 6:14, 101; 35:1; 39:46; 42:11

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is Protector of believers; those under His protection are His friends, who have no fear and receive glad tidings in both lives.
rows.anchor: those under God’s Protection are considered His friends

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph asks not to die except in complete submission to God’s Will and in Abraham’s creed; the Quran also discusses submission more broadly.
rows.anchor: a request to God that he not die except in a state of complete submission to God’s Will

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The verse tells Muhammad that he was absent when Joseph’s brothers plotted and thereby argues for his miraculous knowledge, not learned from people or books, as the unlettered Prophet.
rows.anchor: the miraculous nature of the Prophet’s knowledge, since he was given the unseen details of the story of Joseph without being physically present

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that most people do not believe is linked to 11:17, 13:1, and 40:61.
rows.anchor: For most of mankind . . . are not believers, see 11:17c; 13:1; 40:61

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s concern for people is addressed elsewhere, while the Quran stresses that God alone guides and causes belief.
rows.anchor: it is only God Who guides and only God Who causes people to believe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse echoes 6:90, where the Prophet says he asks no reward and that the Quran is a reminder for the worlds.
rows.anchor: see commentary on 6:90, where the Prophet is instructed to say, I ask not of you any reward for it. It is naught but a reminder for the worlds

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: Heavenly and earthly signs prove the Creator’s being, wisdom, power, and oneness, yet people do not reflect or take a lesson; 6:157 condemns turning away.
rows.anchor: signs and proofs that indicate the being of their Creator as well as His Wisdom, Power, and Oneness, yet they do not reflect upon the meaning

rows.speaker: N
rows.claim: The verse also concerns traces left by vanished peoples, which later generations should learn from but often ignore.
rows.anchor: the previous civilizations and peoples who have passed away and left vestiges behind, from which those who come later are meant to take a lesson

rows.speaker: Kl
rows.claim: The verse is said to concern Makkan idolaters who believed in God while worshipping other gods alongside Him.
rows.anchor: revealed about the Makkan idolaters, who believed in God but also worshipped other gods alongside Him (Kl)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Associating partners is not limited to physical idols; people may idolize desires, power, or ideas.
rows.anchor: other elements that one “idolizes,” such as one’s desires, power, or ideas

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rhetorical warning about feeling safe from punishment is echoed at 16:45–47, 17:68–69, and 67:16–17.
rows.anchor: For the rhetorical question Do they feel secure? (regarding God’s Punishment), see also 16:45–47; 17:68–69; 67:16–17

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: The warning is directed at Makkan idolaters.
rows.anchor: Here the question is about the Makkan idolaters (Ṭs)

rows.speaker: JJ, Ṭs
rows.claim: The overwhelming punishment may mean a thunderbolt.
rows.anchor: The overwhelming punishment refers to a thunderbolt (JJ, Ṭs)

rows.speaker: Bg
rows.claim: Alternatively, the overwhelming punishment may be some enveloping punishment.
rows.anchor: or some kind of enveloping punishment (Bg)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Hour means Judgment Day; its sudden arrival and people’s heedlessness are discussed at 6:31, 7:188, and 21:40.
rows.anchor: the Hour refers to the Day of Judgment. For the sudden nature of the arrival of the Last Day and the general state of heedlessness

rows.speaker: Bg
rows.claim: The Prophet’s way may mean his usual practice.
rows.anchor: way can refer to either the Prophet’s wont (Bg)

rows.speaker: Bg, Z
rows.claim: Alternatively, his way means the religion he brought.
rows.anchor: or the religion he brought (Bg, Z; cf. 16:125)

rows.speaker: Bg
rows.claim: Clear sight means certainty, which distinguishes truth from falsehood.
rows.anchor: By clear sight is meant that by which one can distinguish with certainty between truth and falsehood, namely, certainty (Bg)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Some say the verse answers the Makkan question of why an angel was not sent down to Muhammad.
rows.anchor: revealed as a response to the Makkans’ question in 6:8, Why has not an angel been sent down unto him? (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse relates to the significance of prophets being human and speaking their people’s language, linked to many other passages.
rows.anchor: On the significance of prophets being human beings and speaking the language of their people

rows.speaker: Q, R, Z
rows.claim: Many commentators say town dwellers, considered more knowledgeable and refined, were chosen as prophets, not nomads, and that women were not prophets.
rows.anchor: Many commentators understand the mention of the people of the towns to signify that nomads were never chosen to be prophets

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Some instead read men as meaning human beings rather than angels, without reference to gender.
rows.anchor: they were human beings, not angels (Z; see 17:94–95c)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The call to learn from how earlier peoples ended is linked to 30:9 and 12:105; the Hereafter is better for the reverent, as also discussed at 12:56–57.
rows.anchor: For Have they not journeyed upon the earth and observed how those before them fared in the end? see 30:9c

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets’ human responses to trials are linked to 2:214, 15:97, 21:83, and 26:3.
rows.anchor: For the prophets’ human reactions to the trials they encountered, see 2:214; 15:97; 21:83; 26:3

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s exact vengeance upon the guilty is linked to 32:22.
rows.anchor: ing vengeance upon the guilty people, see 32:22

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: Their stories refers to the stories of messengers mentioned throughout the Quran.
rows.anchor: By their stories is meant the stories of the messengers mentioned throughout the Quran (JJ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran is not fabricated but confirms earlier scriptures, while the Torah is also called an elaboration, guidance, and mercy.
rows.anchor: On the fact that the Quran is not fabricated, but rather confirms the scriptures that came before it
